questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend building alerts last, after the dashboard?
options: Because alert rules are harder to write than dashboards
Because alerts without a working dashboard to validate them against are just guesses at what a reasonable threshold looks like
Because alerting tools require a dashboard to even function
Because alerts are optional and can be skipped entirely
questions.explain: The dashboard lets you see your service's real, normal behavior, which is what lets you set a genuine threshold for an alert rather than guessing at one.

questions.q: What is the minimum recommended metrics instrumentation for the capstone service?
options: Only a single uptime check
A request counter by endpoint/status, a request duration histogram, and one saturation metric on the service's dependency
Every metric the Prometheus client library exposes by default, with no filtering
CPU and memory only
questions.explain: The lesson specifies a minimal but real golden-signals-shaped instrumentation: a request counter, a duration histogram, and a saturation metric on the one dependency.

questions.q: Why does each log line for a request need a correlation ID?
options: To satisfy a compliance requirement unrelated to debugging
So that every log line belonging to one specific request or job run can be found and tied together
Because structured JSON logs are invalid without one
To replace the need for a request counter metric
questions.explain: A correlation ID is what lets you pull every log line related to a single request together, which is essential for diagnosing a specific slow or failed request.

questions.q: What is the recommended panel count for the capstone dashboard, and why?
options: As many as possible, to cover every available metric
Zero — dashboards are optional if alerts exist
4 to 6 panels, because a wall of panels nobody reads is worse than a focused set that answers the key golden-signal questions
Exactly 1 panel showing overall uptime
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly recommends 4-6 focused panels (traffic, latency, errors, saturation, and an optional breakdown), rather than an exhaustive, unreadable wall of metrics.

questions.q: What makes the example alert threshold (p99 latency over 1.5s for 5 minutes) appropriate, according to the lesson?
options: It was copied directly from a public tutorial
It should be derived from watching the student's own service's real, normal behavior rather than guessed or copied
Any arbitrary number works equally well for every service
The threshold doesn't matter as long as the alert has a runbook linked
questions.explain: The lesson stresses that a good alert threshold comes from observing the specific service's actual behavior, not from copying a number that might not fit that service's real traffic or latency profile.
